deckTitle: Pattern C — Dynamic Hybrid Hub-and-Spoke, PSC & Zero-Downtime Tier Migration (Workstream 4)
deckSubtitle: Unifying high-margin Pooled Standard tenants and sovereign Enterprise spokes behind one SaaS URL using Private Service Connect (PSC) and a 3-phase zero-downtime live tier upgrade engine
tldr: One Unified SaaS Front Door for Every Tier: Pattern C fronts both Standard pooled tenants (120 RPM Pool) and regulated Enterprise sovereign spokes (600 RPM Silo) behind a single Global Application Load Balancer URL.

Cryptographic Tier Lookup & Dispatch: Cloud Armor, IAP, and the Cloud Run Hybrid Router inspect the verified OBO/DPoP identity token, query the Firestore routing table, and dispatch traffic per tenant tier.

Unidirectional Private Service Connect (PSC) Bridges: Enterprise requests traverse NAT-based PSC endpoints (`10.10.0.50`) into dedicated spoke projects (`ServiceAttachment`) with zero VPC peering or IP overlap.

3-Phase Zero-Downtime Live Tier Migration (`SHADOW_SYNC` → `ATOMIC_CUTOVER` → `DRAIN_AND_VERIFY`): Promotes a live Standard tenant into a dedicated Enterprise PSC spoke mid-conversation without dropping a single turn.

4/4 Automated Migration & Isolation Assertions Verified: Proves 0ms replication lag at cutover, 0 dropped active sessions, immediate 4,000 → 8,000 thinking budget unlock, and zero global state bleed across instances.

sections.heading: Products used — Hub-and-Spoke Control Plane & Private Service Connect (PSC)
bullets: Central Ingress & Routing Hub (`cymbal-hybrid-hub-prod`): Hosts the Global External ALB, Cloud Armor WAF, IAP OIDC verifier, Cross-Project Agent Registry, and Firestore Tenant Routing Table.

Consumer PSC Endpoint in the Hub (`10.10.0.50`): The Hub VPC (`10.10.0.0/20`) binds an internal Private Service Connect forwarding rule directly to each Enterprise tenant’s spoke ServiceAttachment URI.

Producer ServiceAttachment in Each Spoke (`ACCEPT_MANUAL`): Each Enterprise spoke project exposes its private Cloud Run / GKE agent runtime via a `/24` PSC NAT subnet (`10.40.240.0/24`) whitelisting only the Hub project.

Zero CIDR Overlap & Unidirectional Security: Because PSC performs source NAT at the attachment boundary, all 1,000+ Enterprise spokes can reuse identical `10.40.0.0/20` VPC CIDRs and can never initiate reverse connections into the Hub.

sections.heading: Design considerations — 5-Hop Pipeline Across Hybrid Pooled & PSC Paths

pipelineSteps.title: Edge WAF, OBO/DPoP Minting & Firestore Tier Lookup
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Strips spoofed headers at the Hub ALB, verifies Workspace or Entra ID OIDC tokens, and resolves the tenant’s live routing descriptor (`POOLED` vs. `PSC_SPOKE`) from Firestore.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Signed JWT tenant_id -> Firestore Route (pool:// vs. psc://)
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 401 on Spoofed Header • Zero Client-Controlled Route Override

pipelineSteps.title: Cross-Project Agent Engine Registry & Tool Filtering
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Merges shared pooled capabilities and tenant-owned PSC spoke agents into a single discovery view while hiding Enterprise-only agents from Standard callers.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Visibility Filter Across Hub & Spoke Agent Descriptors
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 403 on Cross-Tenant or Unlicensed Tier Tool Discovery

pipelineSteps.title: Pooled Runtime (4k Cap) vs. Unidirectional PSC Spoke (8k Cap)
pipelineSteps.service: Shared Cloud Run vs. PSC Spoke
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Dispatches Standard turns to the shared pool (120 RPM, 4k thinking cap) and tunnels Enterprise turns across `10.10.0.50` into the dedicated PSC spoke (600 RPM, 8k cap).
pipelineSteps.invariant: Standard: 4k/120 RPM Pool • Enterprise: 8k/600 RPM PSC Spoke
pipelineSteps.gate: Unidirectional PSC NAT Prevents Spoke-to-Hub Lateral Movement

pipelineSteps.title: Pooled Model Armor Floor vs. Spoke Custom Regulatory DLP
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Applies baseline prompt-injection and PCI screening in the shared pool while executing custom regulatory NLCs (OCC/HIPAA) and dedicated DLP templates inside each spoke.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Per-Tier Safety Templates + Egress IBAN/SWIFT/PAN Redaction
pipelineSteps.gate: HTTP 400 on Prompt Injection • HTTP 422 on Regulatory NLC Breach

pipelineSteps.title: AlloyDB RLS / CMEK Spoke Vault & CDC Shadow Replication
pipelineSteps.mechanism: Isolates Standard rows via AlloyDB RLS, isolates Enterprise state in CMEK spoke databases, and streams CDC state during live tier promotions with unified BigQuery OTel billing.
pipelineSteps.invariant: Pooled RLS <-> Spoke CMEK Vault • 0ms Lag CDC Cutover
pipelineSteps.gate: 0 Unauthorized Rows • HTTP 423 on Spoke CMEK Revocation

bullets: Hop 1 — Central Hub Authentication & Tier Resolution: Verifies OIDC identity at the Hub edge and looks up the authoritative pool:// or psc:// route in Firestore.
Hop 2 — Cross-Project Federated Agent Catalog: Resolves shared tools and private spoke agents while enforcing strict tenant visibility.
Hop 3 — Tiered Compute & PSC Dispatch: Routes Standard tenants to the shared 4k-cap pool and tunnels Enterprise tenants over Private Service Connect to their 8k-cap spoke.
Hop 4 — Tiered Model Armor & DLP: Enforces shared safety floors in the pool and custom regulatory NLC/DLP policies inside each Enterprise spoke.
Hop 5 — Hybrid Storage & Unified FinOps: Pairs pooled AlloyDB RLS and dedicated CMEK spoke databases with continuous BigQuery OTel chargeback.

diagrams.title: Pattern C Terraform PSC Resource Graph: Hub VPC → Consumer Endpoint → Spoke ServiceAttachment
talkingPoints: Illustrates the dual-provider Terraform module (`4.6-terraform-hybrid-psc-blueprint/main.tf`) that wires cross-project Private Service Connect.
Zone 1 (`google.hub` Network): Provisions `cymbal-pattern-c-hub-vpc` and `10.10.0.0/20` subnet with Private Google Access enabled.
Zone 3 (`google.spoke` NAT & Producer): Provisions spoke VPC (`10.40.0.0/20`), `PSC_NAT` subnet (`10.40.240.0/24`), and `google_compute_service_attachment`.
Zone 4 (`google.hub` Consumer Bridge): Reserves internal IP `10.10.0.50` and binds `google_compute_forwarding_rule` directly to the spoke attachment.
Zone 2 (Firestore Output Binding): Exports `spoke_psc_service_attachment_uri` and `hub_psc_consumer_ip` directly into the Firestore routing table.

takeaways: Route Isolation Instead of Duplicating Products: Serve every customer tier behind one unified SaaS domain and control plane while dispatching requests dynamically to pooled or sovereign boundaries.

Bind Tier Routing Strictly to Cryptographic Identity: Derive routing decisions exclusively from the Hop 1 OBO/DPoP token and Firestore routing table so callers can never spoof headers to access Enterprise spokes.

Scale to 1,000+ Enterprise Spokes with Private Service Connect: NAT-based PSC ServiceAttachments eliminate VPC peering quotas, allow identical spoke CIDRs (`10.40.0.0/20`), and enforce one-way hub-to-spoke calls.

Turn Tier Upgrades into a Zero-Downtime Self-Service Feature: Use the 3-phase migration state machine (`SHADOW_SYNC` → `ATOMIC_CUTOVER` → `DRAIN_AND_VERIFY`) to promote live sessions without dropping a single turn.
Isolate Runtime Profile State per Instance: Deep-copy tenant routing profiles per engine instance (`F-09`) so dynamic tier promotions never cause cross-tenant configuration bleed.

In this session on Workstream 4, we explore Pattern C—our Dynamic Hybrid Hub-and-Spoke architecture—which combines the cost-efficiency of Pattern A’s shared pool with the regulatory isolation of Pattern B’s sovereign silos behind one unified SaaS front door, complete with zero-downtime live tier upgrades.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act I — Customer Use Cases, Competing Tenant Profiles & Cloud Stack
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: Following our opening roadmap on Slide 1, we always start with the customer first—because an architecture only creates business value when it solves real customer constraints.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: Think about the customer lifecycle every successful SaaS business experiences, shown here on this slide. A company like RetailStream signs up on Monday as a standard commercial customer in our Shared Pool because they want instant onboarding and low cost. Six months later, they expand their contract to an enterprise regulated tier and need their own dedicated sovereign spoke. Business leaders cannot ask that customer to change their URL, re-authenticate their users, or accept a weekend maintenance outage—and technical leaders need a way to route both pooled and siloed tenants seamlessly from a single control plane.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act II (Level 3 Zoom) — 5-Actor Chronological Request Lifeline
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: Taking the physical components we just saw on Slide 5, this slide brings the architecture to life by tracing a single customer turn in chronological order.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: How do we move a live customer from the yellow Shared Pool to a red Sovereign Spoke while their employees are actively chatting with the AI agent? This chronological timeline shows our four-stage zero-downtime upgrade choreography across five actors. First, during Shadow Sync, we copy their historical AlloyDB rows and memory namespaces into the new spoke in the background while live traffic keeps running in the pool. Second, our verifier checks 100% row-count and cryptographic hash parity. Third, we execute an Atomic Cutover that flips their routing pointer in zero milliseconds between turns. Fourth, we drain in-flight requests and retire the old pooled rows.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatComesNext: Having watched the request move from hop to hop on Slide 6, a technical architect or security officer will naturally ask: what actually changes inside the data packet on the wire so a caller can never fake their company ID? Let's zoom all the way in on Slide 7.

slideSpeakerNotes.title: Act II (Level 4 Zoom) — Wire-Level Payload & Cryptographic Context Transformation
slideSpeakerNotes.whyHere: This slide completes our four-level architectural zoom in Act II—taking us from the step-by-step timeline on Slide 6 right inside the JSON message envelope traveling across the wire.
slideSpeakerNotes.whatIsHappening: Here you can see that zero-millisecond atomic cutover happening inside the actual routing packet on the wire.
